doc.title: Data Types and Conversion
doc.paragraph: Every value in Adaptive Script has a data type, and that data type never changes behind your back. An integer stays an integer, a string stays a string, and the text "false" is a string, not the boolean false. When you want a value of another data type, you ask for it, and the script says exactly where that happens. This section shows how to write a value of each data type, how to test, assert, and convert, and the rules a few families of data types follow.
The full list of data types, with a description of each, is in the Data Types chapter of the Architecture Guide.

section.title: Writing a Value of Each Data Type
section.paragraph: Some data types have a literal of their own, like 42 or true. The others are written as a typed literal: a string literal followed immediately by the data type id, or by a shorter form of it. Let's start with a value most scripts need sooner or later, a point in time:

Both lines make the same dateTime value. The text is read when the script is compiled, using the same parser the data type uses everywhere else, so a typo is caught before the script ever runs: "nope"dt is a compile error, Invalid dateTime typed literal. The following table shows how to write a value of each data type:

row.column: function (x) { return x; }, or a built-in by name (add)
json('{"a":1}'), script("1 + 1"): the function holds the source text, and compile or eval uses it

section.paragraph: A few rules for typed literals:

list.item: Either quote works, and there is no space between the closing quote and the suffix.
String escapes are processed first, so a backslash in the text is written \\. That is why a regular expression literal, /a\d+/, is usually easier to read than "a\\d+"re.
A suffix that is not a data type with a typed literal is a compile error, such as 'foo' is not a typed literal suffix.
Text data types check their text too: an ia5String must be ASCII, an objectPath must be a path, an rfc822Name needs a local part, an @, and a domain, and an x500Name must be a distinguished name.
Typed literals are part of Adaptive Script. They are not used in JSON or relaxed JSON, after a template string, or as a property name.

section.paragraph: When decompile writes a value, it uses these same forms, always with the full data type id, so what it writes compiles back to the same value. If you would like to see every suffix the environment knows about, including those an extension adds, retrieve the _AdaptiveTypedLiteralSuffix_ objects from adapter afw.

section.title: Test, Assert, and Convert
section.paragraph: Once you have a value, there are three things you may want to do with its data type, and each one has its own form:

row.column: a new value of the other data type

section.paragraph: is_T(v) takes any value and answers whether it is a T. It never throws, and it is false for undefined. So is<date>("2026-10-11") is false, because that value is a string, and is<date>("2026-10-11"date) is true. A built-in function is a function just like one you write: is<function>(add) is true.

v as T says "this value is a T." If it is, you get the same value back, unchanged. If it is not, the script stops with an argument_error, and the message tells you how to get the value you probably meant:

as never converts, and it is checked when the script runs, whether or not type checking is turned on. It binds like a comparison operator, so a + b as integer asserts the sum. When you want to keep going after the assertion, put it in parentheses: (v as integer) + 1 or (v as object).name. For now T is a data type, or a type alias of one.

null is a data type of its own, so null as string is an error and null as null is fine. That is stricter than an annotation: let s: string = null; is allowed unless strictNullChecks is on. When a value may be missing, test it first with is_nullish(v).

to_T(v) makes a new value of data type T. From a string, it reads the text with the same parser a typed literal uses, and bad text is a conversion_error. That makes to_dateTime(s) the run-time form of "…"dateTime, for text that comes from somewhere else:
section.code: to_date("2026-10-11"); // a date to_date("nope"); // conversion_error to_integer("007"); // 7 to_integer("1.5"); // conversion_error: not integer text to_integer(1.9); // 1, toward zero to_double("5"); // 5.0 to_double(5); // 5.0 to_string(42); // "42"
section.paragraph: to_double and to_integer read numbers the way XML Schema writes them, so "5", ".5", and "007" are all good number text. to_base64Binary(s) and to_hexBinary(s) read text that is already encoded; to encode a string's own bytes, use encode_as_base64Binary(s).

Data type names are not conversion functions. dateTime("…") and integer(x) are compile errors, and the message names the typed literal or to_T function to use instead. A few names that build a value are functions: boolean(v), string(…), array(…), object(v), and the functions that hold source text, such as json, script, and template.

There are two ways to get a boolean from another value, and they answer different questions. boolean(v) asks whether a value is "truthy": an empty string, zero, NaN, null, and undefined are false, and everything else is true, including every object and array. string_to_boolean(s) reads text that spells a boolean:
string_to_boolean accepts true and false in any case, 1 and 0, and t and f; any other text is a conversion_error.

Conditions want a boolean, not a truthy value. The condition of an if, while, or ?:, and the operands of !, &&, and ||, must be booleans: if (count) is an argument_error when count is an integer. Say what you mean, with if (count > 0) or if (boolean(name)).

You will see <T> after a function name in two ways. For a polymorphic function, such as to_string, add, or compile, T is the data type of the first argument. You usually leave it out, because the function picks the right version from the argument: to_string(1) runs to_string<integer>. For is, T is the data type you are testing for, so it is required: is<dateTime>(v) is is_dateTime(v).

section.title: No Hidden Conversions
section.paragraph: Anywhere a data type is declared, the value is checked, and it is never quietly converted to fit. This holds for the parameters of built-in functions, and for the let, const, parameters, and return types you annotate in your own scripts. When the value does not fit, the message suggests the conversion:

list.item: + on strings takes strings only. Write "a" + to_string(1), concat("a", 1), or string("a", 1), all "a1".
A single value is not an array of one: add_entries(a, 1) is an error, where push(a, 1) or add_entries(a, [1]) is what you want.
An object property name is a string and an array index is an integer, so o[1] is an error on an object.

section.paragraph: Data types, arrays of a data type (integer[]), and unions of these (integer | string) are checked whenever the script runs. Object shapes, tuples, and function types are checked when type checking is turned on; see Types.

section.title: Integers and Doubles
section.paragraph: Integers and doubles are separate data types, and arithmetic and comparison take two of the same kind. 1 + 1.0 is an error, and so is 1 == 1.0 (Data types do not match). Write 1.0 + 1.0, or to_double(1) + 1.0.

An integer is 64 bits and its arithmetic is exact. 7 / 2 is 3, and 2 ** 3 is the integer 8. A result that does not fit, such as #integerMax + 1, an integer divided by zero, or 2 ** -1, is an error rather than a wrong answer or a double.
Doubles follow IEEE 754: 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity and 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN. A double is written as text in its shortest form that reads back as the same double, with an exponent: to_string(0.1) is "1.0E-1".

If you would rather have those be errors, add #compile strictDouble; to the script, or set the flag compile:strictDouble. Then IEEE 754's invalid operation and division by zero are errors: 0.0 / 0.0, 1.0 / 0.0, Infinity - Infinity, sqrt(-1.0), and log(0.0), and <, <=, >, and >= with a NaN are errors too. Everything else stays the same: an overflow still gives an infinity, a NaN operand passes through arithmetic, and == with a NaN is simply false. The pragma applies to the script it is in, wherever its functions are called from.

section.title: Dates, Times, and Durations
section.paragraph: date, dateTime, time, dayTimeDuration, and yearMonthDuration read and write the text forms of XML Schema 1.1. A dateTime may have a time zone (Z or an offset such as +02:00), and two values with a time zone are compared by the instant they name:

When one value has a time zone and the other does not, the one without is taken to be in the local time zone of the process. A duration is written in its canonical form, so to_string("PT36H"dayTimeDuration) is "P1DT12H". Functions such as add_dayTimeDuration and subtract_yearMonthDuration do date arithmetic; the Function Reference lists them with each data type.

section.title: Names and Addresses
section.paragraph: anyURI, dnsName, ipAddress, rfc822Name, and x500Name are text with rules of their own about when two values are equal. An rfc822Name (an email address) ignores case in its domain, so "A@Example.com"rfc822Name equals "A@example.com"rfc822Name. An x500Name compares as a distinguished name, and dnsName and ipAddress ignore case.

These data types have no order: < on two dnsName values is an error. To ask whether a name falls under another, such as an address in a domain or a name under a branch of a directory, use the _match functions of the data type, for example rfc822Name_match and x500Name_match.

section.title: Values as Text
section.paragraph: There are three ways to turn a value into text, and each is meant for a different reader:

list.item: to_string(v) writes the value itself as text, the way you would show it to a person: to_string("2026-10-11"date) is "2026-10-11". A script function written with string(f) or to_string(f) is its own source.
stringify(v) writes JSON, for another program. JSON has no undefined, so a property whose value is undefined is left out: stringify({a: undefined, b: 1}) is {"b":1}.

decompile(v) writes Adaptive Script, with typed literals and compiler literals, so the text compiles back to the same value: decompile({d: "2026-10-11"date, n: #nan}) is {"d":"2026-10-11"date,"n":#nan}.
